items.description_text: Homecoming Becoming the Place We Belong Homecoming is an international training course exploring embodied belonging – within ourselves, in relationship with others, and as part of the living world. It invites participants to slow down, return to their centre, and reconnect with the body as a place of grounding, safety and aliveness. Through embodiment, movement, authentic relating, silence and nature connection, participants explore what it means to feel at home in themselves and how to create spaces where others can experience acceptance and belonging. The journey nurtures self-awareness, emotional regulation, authentic connection and a deeper relationship with the Earth – remembering our way back to ourselves, each other and the world we belong to. A key focus of the training is belonging as an embodied experience. Participants explore what safety, acceptance and connection actually feel like in the body, and how we can return to our centre while staying open to relationship. Through nurturing practices, bodywork and shared rituals, they experience how warmth, presence and trust can allow us to become home to ourselves and to each other. The training also explores the body in relationship with the group and with nature, creating space for silence, mystery and deeper listening. Participants practice meeting themselves with greater self-love and acceptance, while developing the capacity to offer grounded, heartfelt presence and guidance to others. These experiences are translated into practical approaches for youth work, supporting participants in creating spaces where young people can feel seen, welcomed and free to be themselves. Homecoming invites youth workers to carry this sense of belonging back into their communities. items.description_text: LEC (Love Every Challenge) is a 5-day leadership and self-development training for youth workers, trainers, volunteers, and educators who want to deepen self-awareness, strengthen resilience, and bring new methods back into their youth work. Working with young people can be rewarding — but also exhausting. Many youth workers feel stuck, overwhelmed, or unsure about their next steps. LEC offers a space to pause, reflect, and recharge while also learning tools that can be applied directly in their personal life and non-formal education settings. At the heart of LEC is the invitation to: “Become a leader you wish to follow.” This means learning to lead from your values, cultivating emotional intelligence, and embodying the resilience and courage that you wish to inspire in others. The training is based on the Swedish Value Based Leadership programme, enriched with synergy methods and our own 20 years of experience in experiential learning. We combine: Adventure & outdoors: stretching comfort zones, building trust, and exploring leadership through symbolic challenges in nature. Embodiment & community: movement, storytelling, role play, and sharing circles to explore emotions, values, and inner compass. Experience & reflection: learning by doing, then transferring insights into daily life and youth work practice. Participants will: Develop personal resilience and self-leadership, essential in preventing burnout. Gain practical tools for group facilitation, reflection processes, and working with challenges. Strengthen their emotional intelligence and ability to support young people in transitions and difficulties. Join a community of youth workers from Latvia and other European countries, sharing experiences and building networks for future cooperation. items.description_text: Mindful Youth – Building Resilience Together is an Erasmus+ Training Course designed for youth workers, youth leaders, trainers, educators, facilitators and other professionals actively involved in non-formal learning and youth work. The training focuses on strengthening young people’s resilience, emotional well-being and ability to cope with stress and everyday challenges. It responds to the growing need for practical approaches that youth workers can integrate into their regular work with young people, particularly when supporting those experiencing stress, emotional difficulties, social pressure or challenging life situations. Throughout the training, participants will explore mindfulness, emotional regulation, stress management, self-awareness and resilience-building through experiential and non-formal education methods. The programme will combine practical exercises, group work, reflection, discussions, creative activities, mindfulness practices and peer learning. Participants will have opportunities both to experience the methods themselves and to reflect on how they can adapt and apply them with young people in their own organisations and communities. The activity is particularly targeted at applicants who are currently active in youth work and/or non-formal education and who are interested in incorporating well-being and resilience-building approaches into their professional or voluntary practice. Previous expertise in mindfulness is not required, but participants should be motivated to actively engage in the programme, exchange experiences with an international group and transfer the acquired methods into their local youth work. By the end of the training, participants are expected to have a broader understanding of resilience and well-being in youth work, an increased awareness of their own well-being as youth workers, and a set of practical, adaptable tools and methods that can be used in non-formal learning settings with young people. As modern humans, we have created an existence where Logos is largely dominant. The logic of the mind controls and manages life, resources, and the environment, and thus we have estranged ourselves from the world of Myth. The Mythic world is a portal into living life in a more sacred way, more aligned with our Deep Self, the original instructions on how to live on the Earth, our Souls, and the Great Mystery that holds the web of life. items.description_text: Career UP – helping young people navigate career choices “Career UP” is an international training course for youth workers and other professionals working with young people in non-formal education settings. It is designed for those who want to strengthen their ability to support young people in understanding themselves, exploring career possibilities, and making realistic career decisions. Young people today face more choices, rapidly changing labour-market realities, and an overwhelming amount of information. Career UP approaches career guidance not as one final “right choice”, but as a lifelong and evolving process shaped by personal values, skills, strengths, experiences, and external factors. During the 6-day training course, participants will explore practical ways to support young people throughout this process. The programme combines non-formal education, experiential learning, reflection, peer exchange, facilitation practice, and hands-on activities. Participants will work with methods and tools that can be directly adapted to their daily work with young people. The training will focus on: supporting young people in self-understanding and self-awareness; helping them identify their values, skills, and strengths; facilitating realistic career decision-making; dealing with uncertainty, decision anxiety, and information overload; supporting young people in moving from planning to action; strengthening resilience and adaptability; using non-formal methods, facilitation techniques, and digital tools in career guidance. The training is intended for youth workers, educators, social workers, counsellors, project coordinators, mentors, community leaders, and activists. items.description_text: Our bodies can often notice what is happening before we are able to name it. A change in posture, a feeling of tension, an impulse to move away or come closer can all provide valuable information about our emotions, needs and relationships. Learning to recognise these signals can help us become more present and responsive - both in our own lives and when working with groups. Rooted is an invitation to slow down, turn inward, and explore what allows us to stay connected - to ourselves, to others, and to what truly matters to us. Through Nonviolent Communication and embodiment practices, we will explore the relationship between our inner experience and the way we meet the world around us. In this training, NVC is approached not simply as a communication method, but as an embodied way of being - a practice of listening deeply to ourselves and others, recognising emotions and needs, and responding with greater awareness and choice. Through movement, body awareness, reflection and authentic connection, we will explore how we can become more grounded in ourselves while staying open and present in relationship. Throughout the training, we will explore how embodied approaches can broaden the ways we understand certain situations, connect with ourselves and others. By developing greater sensitivity to what is happening within the body, we can learn to respond to situations with more awareness, flexibility and care. Rooted in both NVC and embodiment, this training invites you to move beyond simply knowing communication concepts and towards experiencing them in your own body - cultivating greater self-awareness, groundedness and connection that can be carried into your everyday relationships and work with others. ___________________________ OBJECTIVES -integrating Nonviolent Communication beyond techniques, cultivating it as an inner attitude and way of being -developing own self-awareness, clarity and self-compassion -strengthening capacity to listen with empathy and learning

Methods for assessing needs. A clearer way to set and measure objectives. A wider repertoire of non-formal methods that works with groups who are hard to reach. items.description_text: A waiting room. A youth centre. A public square. A restroom. A courtroom. Most spaces used by young people are designed by adults. Adults decide what is needed, what feels safe and what feels welcoming. But how often do we ask young people what they think? And more importantly, how often do we invite them to create these spaces with us? The idea for this training comes from a cocreation project in which four unaccompanied minors worked with judges, guardians and children's rights experts to redesign a courtroom for the Belgian Council for Alien Law Litigation. Their ideas helped create a space that felt calmer, clearer and more respectful. The project showed that when young people are treated as equal partners, everyone benefits, including the adults who use and work in these spaces. Why does this matter? Many STEAM activities start with a predefined outcome: build a bridge, create a vehicle, follow these instructions. Storybuilders Lab explores a different approach. The facilitator defines the learning intention, but participants influence the story, identify the problem and decide what needs to be created. The methodology follows a simple learning cycle: STORY → QUESTION → IDEAS → CHALLENGE → DESIGN → MAKE → TEST → IMPROVE → REFLECT → STORY CONTINUES Participants will learn how to use story triggers, mystery objects and open questions to generate curiosity and meaningful challenges. They will explore Story Democracy, a participatory method for collecting, combining and developing different ideas so that the direction of a project is not predetermined by the facilitator or dominated by the strongest voices in the group. A central part of the course is hands-on prototyping. Participants will work with accessible materials such as cardboard, recyclable materials and simple construction tools to turn ideas into physical prototypes. Makedo or similar cardboard-construction tools may be used where available, but no specialised equipment is required. The focus is not on creating a perfect final object. Participants practise an iterative process of: Make → Test → Notice → Change → Test again This allows them to explore how experimentation, “failure”, debugging and redesign can become valuable learning experiences in youth work. The project aims to: explore Europe as a philosophical, historical and ethical project; strengthen youth workers’ understanding of European values, human rights and citizenship; develop skills to facilitate dialogue on complex and sensitive topics; learn how to manage conflicting opinions and polarization constructively; provide practical methods to foster critical thinking and participation among young people. items.description_text: This training is part of the “Engage, Connect and Empower Local Youth Councils in Europe” (ECE-LYCE) project. It addresses the mismatch identified between current LYC outreach efforts and their broader local demographics. Recognising that a significant majority of councils struggle with public relations and require advanced skills in digital branding and storytelling, this course instructs participants on how to move past dry, bureaucratic announcements toward dynamic, narrative-driven digital communication. The curriculum focuses on inclusive outreach strategies to break the inner "activism bubble" and intentionally engage historically underrepresented, marginalised, or non-active youth populations. To ensure these diversification efforts result in long-term retention rather than immediate dropout, the training combines external promotion with internal support systems. Participants will learn about structured onboarding protocols, peer-to-peer "buddy systems," and membership rotation models to stop the fragile practice of informal knowledge loss when senior members leave the LYC. With these integrated communication and mentoring frameworks LYCs will be equipped to broaden their visibility to the wider population and build sustainable channels for diverse civic participation. The methodology is based on non-formal education principles, combining peer learning, group work, simulations, case studies, reflection activities, and exchange of practices among participants from different local realities.

items.description_text: What is the course about? The course explores the role of mentors in European Solidarity Corps (ESC) volunteering projects and highlights the important contribution mentoring makes to the overall quality of the volunteering experience. Mentoring is an essential form of personal support for all participants involved in volunteering activities. As outlined in the European Solidarity Corps Programme Guide, every young volunteer should have access to appropriate and meaningful mentoring support throughout their experience. For this reason, the course places particular emphasis on developing mentors’ competences through interactive learning, reflection, exchange of experiences, and peer-to-peer learning. Aim The main aim of the training course is to strengthen participants’ mentoring competences through interactive activities, peer-to-peer learning, exchange of practices, and reflection, contributing to improved quality in European Solidarity Corps volunteering projects. Objectives The training course aims to: Develop a deeper understanding of the volunteering strand of the European Solidarity Corps Programme and create a shared understanding of the key quality aspects of ESC volunteering projects. Provide a supportive space for participants to exchange good practices, experiences, challenges, and different realities related to mentoring in volunteering projects. items.description_text: About the project Many young people spend increasing amounts of time indoors and online, while nature can be a vital source of connection, well-being and resilience. This training helps youth workers experience nature as an active part of the learning process, not just a backdrop. Participants slow down, observe, and explore their own relationship with nature — then critically reflect on what place nature holds in their youth work now, and could hold in the future. Aim & objectives The training supports youth workers in integrating nature-based learning and eco-friendly practices into their everyday work, strengthening competences in facilitation, activity design, reflection, and translating insights into practice. It follows five steps: Connect (building a safe foundation with self, others and nature), Experience (exploring nature-based methods for well-being and resilience), Critically explore (examining personal nature values and their role in practice), Design (creating activities using a practical template), and Take action (developing a concrete plan for their own work and organisation). Learning approach The training is based on Nature-Based Learning (NBL): learning in, from and about nature, spending as much time outdoors as possible. Through experiential learning — slowing down, observing, and harvesting insights — participants connect experience to practice and move toward concrete action. Central to the approach is a reciprocal relationship with nature: learning from it while exploring how this connection inspires care and responsibility.

items.description_text: Humour is already present in youth work practice - but it's rarely used as a deliberate, structured tool. "Humour is Serious Business" (HiSB) is a 6-day Erasmus+ KA153-YOU training course (27 November - 3 December 2026, Hollókő, Hungary) that will help you turn something you probably already do instinctively into an intentional, ethical, and effective competence for engaging young people. This training is aimed specifically at practitioners in the field of non-formal learning and youth work - not at the general public. You should apply if you are a youth worker (professional or voluntary), a youth leader, a young person (18+) with leadership potential already identified by your organisation, or a practitioner with relevant expertise who works with young people (e.g. a coach, mentor or tutor), even if youth work is not your primary profession. Through non-formal methods - World Café, simulations and role play, clowning and improvisation, team building, and daily reflection groups - you will explore the many different types of humour, examine cultural differences in how humour is used, reflect on your own sense of humour, and develop concrete post-programme actions to bring back to your own community. Every participant leaves with a Personal Development Plan and the chance to earn a Youthpass. HiSB is delivered by an experienced international Training Team and hosted by MAVISZ (Hungary), together with partner organisations in Poland, Portugal, Armenia, Serbia, Latvia, Croatia, Montenegro and Spain. 36 participants will take part, 4 per sending country. Full details, including the daily programme, participant support structure, and reimbursement process, are in the Info Pack: https://mavisz.my.canva.site/hisb2026

items.description_text: Create with Makey Makey: From Curiosity to Creation through 5E and STEAM is an interactive e-learning training designed for youth workers, trainers, facilitators, educators and professionals who want to use creative technology as a tool for participation, experimentation and active learning. The training goes beyond learning how to use Makey Makey as a technical device. Its main focus is on how Makey Makey can be integrated into meaningful non-formal learning experiences by combining STEAM education, the 5E instructional model and interactive methodologies. Throughout the course, participants will experience the five stages of the 5E model: Engage, Explore, Explain, Elaborate and Evaluate. Each stage will be connected with practical Makey Makey activities and non-formal learning methods. Participants will begin with curiosity-based challenges and exploratory activities, investigating conductivity and discovering how everyday objects, water, fruit, aluminium foil, graphite, recycled materials and other conductive surfaces can become computer inputs. They will then explore how Makey Makey can be connected with Scratch and used to create interactive digital experiences such as sound installations, interactive posters, musical instruments, collaborative games, storytelling activities, art projects and team-building challenges. The STEAM approach will be embedded throughout the training: Science through conductivity, circuits and experimentation. Technology through Makey Makey and Scratch. Engineering through designing and testing interactive systems. Arts through music, storytelling, visual expression and creative design. Mathematics through sequencing, patterns, logic and problem-solving. The training is based on non-formal education principles and prioritises learning by doing, collaboration, experimentation, peer learning, reflection and active participation. items.description_text: Project Summary: Leveraging ICT and Social Media for Youth Inclusion and Participation Aim of the Project: The project is designed to equip youth workers with digital skills and tools to strengthen civic participation and engage young people through Information and Communication Technology (ICT). A core aim is to promote civic engagement through digital tools. Objectives: Strengthen Digital Competencies: Provide practical training in ICT, social media engagement, and digital content creation. Youth workers will be trained to guide young people in critical media analysis, recognizing misinformation, and using digital platforms for youth activism and community participation. Ensure Inclusion and Equal Access: Develop strategies to engage marginalized and disadvantaged young people who face barriers to digital participation. Encourage Innovation: Introduce interactive, gamified, and blended learning approaches to make digital engagement more dynamic and adaptive. Strengthen Transnational Cooperation: Establish a European Digital Youth Work Network for collaboration and knowledge exchange, and develop a Digital Civic Engagement Toolkit with practical resources. Outcome: The project aims to significantly enhance the digital skills of youth workers and strengthen youth engagement through the use of digital tools for non-formal education and social participation. It seeks to expand civic participation through youth-led activism and make digital youth work more accessible and inclusive for young people from diverse and disadvantaged backgrounds. The project's sustainability will be ensured through the creation of a European-wide network of digital youth workers and an open-access toolkit, ensuring that the methodologies remain relevant and scalable.

items.description_text: The ENRMSC European Dialogue & Capacity-Building Forum 2027 will take place in Warsaw, Poland, in April 2027. The forum will bring together young refugees, migrants and stateless changemakers, youth workers, youth leaders, researchers, academics, civil society organisations, public institutions and other practitioners working with young people. The forum is built around a simple question: How can we move from young people being affected by systems to young people meaningfully shaping knowledge, opportunities, policies and solutions? The programme will explore meaningful participation, access to education and professional opportunities, community leadership, research and evidence, youth engagement, advocacy and collaboration between communities and institutions. Participants will take part in interactive discussions, panel sessions, workshops and facilitated group activities. The programme will combine knowledge exchange with practical capacity-building and opportunities for participants to develop new connections and potential European cooperation. A particular focus will be placed on recognising lived experience as expertise. Young refugees, migrants and stateless people will not only participate as beneficiaries but as contributors, knowledge holders, community leaders and partners in shaping discussions and recommendations. The forum will also connect participants with relevant European opportunities, networks and potential partners, including opportunities related to youth work, education, research, leadership and civic participation. The event is particularly relevant to people working in non-formal learning and youth work who engage with young people from refugee, migrant and stateless backgrounds. The guiding principle of the forum is: “Nothing About Us Without Us.” The forum is currently being developed by the European Network of Refugee, Migrant and Stateless Changemakers (ENRMSC), a refugee-, migrant- and stateless-led European civil society organisation.

items.description_text: Why this programme? Young people increasingly experience the world through digital, visual, interactive and participatory media. At the same time, heritage education can sometimes remain centred on traditional formats: guided tours, exhibitions, historical information and passive observation. This creates an opportunity for youth work. New media can provide alternative entry points into heritage, allowing young people to: explore places and stories through immersive experiences; discover hidden or forgotten narratives; connect personal and community memories with wider European heritage; question dominant interpretations of history; create their own narratives; collaborate across cultures; transform physical spaces into interactive learning environments. The programme therefore does not aim to turn youth trainers into technology specialists. Instead, it aims to help them become creative facilitators who know when, why and how to use technology to create meaningful learning experiences. General aim To strengthen the capacity of youth trainers to use new media and emerging technologies as tools for heritage awareness, intercultural learning, creativity and youth participation. Specific objectives By the end of the training, participants will be able to: Explore contemporary approaches to cultural heritage and heritage awareness. Identify opportunities for using immersive and interactive media in youth work. Experiment with VR, AR, 360° media, projection mapping, interactive installations, digital storytelling and other creative technologies. Design non-formal education activities connecting young people with local, national and European heritage. Use storytelling and participatory methodologies to make heritage more relevant to young people. Encourage young people to question, reinterpret and remix heritage narratives. It addresses two main needs: Strengthening the skills of facilitators and community leaders so they can design and implement educational projects with strong social and ecological impact. Actively engaging young people in meaningful, concrete, and transformative projects. The project uses the living garden as an educational, sensory, and cooperative tool, helping to recreate connections between humans and ecosystems. These spaces become platforms for social transformation, civic education, and territorial resilience. It is based on active pedagogy that promotes autonomy, local engagement, and the transversal skills required for the ecological transition.
